title: Check yourself: what a subclass inherits

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: `Vehicle` declares `int wheels = 4;` and `String describe() { return wheels + " wheels"; }`. `Motorbike extends Vehicle` declares `int wheels = 2;` and nothing else. After `Vehicle v = new Motorbike();`, what do `v.describe()` and `((Motorbike) v).wheels` give?

options.text: describe() gives "4 wheels" and the cast reads 2, since each read uses the field of the type it is compiled against
options.says: a field is not overridden: describe() is compiled inside Vehicle and reads Vehicle's field, and the cast's declared type Motorbike picks Motorbike's

options.text: describe() gives "4 wheels" and the cast reads 4, since a field read keeps the variable's declared type even through a cast
options.says: the cast changes the declared type of the expression to Motorbike, so it reads Motorbike's field, 2

options.text: describe() gives "2 wheels" and the cast reads 2, since the object's class picks the field, as it picks an overriding method
options.says: only overridable instance methods are chosen by the object; a field is bound by the compiler to the declared type, so describe() reads Vehicle's 4

options.text: describe() gives "2 wheels" and the cast reads 4, since a method reads the object's field but a cast keeps the variable's type
options.says: describe() reads Vehicle's field, 4, because fields are bound to the declared type; the cast's declared type is Motorbike, so it reads 2

origin.section: A Field Is Hidden, Not Overridden: the Declared Type Picks Which One Is Read

questions.stem: `Shape` has `double area()`. `Polygon extends Shape` overrides `area()`, and `Square extends Polygon` overrides it again. Inside `Square.area()`, a developer who needs `Shape`'s version writes `return ((Shape) this).area();`. What happens when `area()` is called on a `Square`?

options.text: It returns Shape's result, since the cast sends the call to the version declared in Shape
options.says: a cast changes the declared type, not the object; the call is still dispatched to Square's own area()

options.text: It returns Polygon's result, since the cast moves the call one class up, as a super call would
options.says: only super.area() skips the object's own override, and it is written with super, not a cast; the cast is dispatched to Square.area()

options.text: It fails at run time, since the cast still sends the call to the object's own area(), over and over
options.says: the cast doesn't change the object, so Square.area() calls itself until the stack runs out with StackOverflowError

options.text: It fails at compile time, since the cast of this can't reach a method its own class overrides
options.says: the cast compiles; the failure comes at run time, as the AuditLogger example shows

origin.section: super.m() Calls the Superclass's Version, and Nothing Reaches Past It

questions.stem: `Notifier` has `public void send(String text)`. So that only its own package can send, `QuietNotifier extends Notifier` overrides it as package-private: `@Override void send(String text) { ... }`. What happens?

options.text: It compiles, and code in other packages can't call send on a QuietNotifier, since the override's access applies to its own class
options.says: an override may not narrow access; javac refuses it with 'attempting to assign weaker access privileges'

options.text: It compiles, and code holding a Notifier still reaches the override, since access is checked against the declared type
options.says: the reason is why narrowing is forbidden, but javac refuses the override, so nothing reaches it

options.text: It doesn't compile, since no override may make the method less accessible, with or without @Override
options.says: an override may not narrow access, and nothing is wider than public; a method with the same signature overrides whether it is annotated or not

options.text: It doesn't compile, since @Override forbids the change, and without @Override it compiles as a new method
options.says: a method with the same signature overrides whether or not it carries @Override, and javac refuses the narrower access either way

origin.section: An Override Can Widen Access but Not Narrow It, So a Subclass Can't Take a Method Away

questions.stem: `com.example.billing.Invoice` has `protected long totalCents;`. In `com.example.reports`, `AuditedInvoice extends Invoice` has `long diff(Invoice other) { return totalCents - other.totalCents; }`. In `com.example.billing`, `Exporter`, which extends nothing, reads `invoice.totalCents` from an `Invoice invoice`. Which of the two compiles?

options.text: Both compile, since only classes outside the package that don't extend Invoice are kept out
options.says: in another package a subclass reaches a protected member only through references of its own type; other.totalCents is read through an Invoice

options.text: Neither compiles, since a protected member is open to subclasses only, and Exporter is no subclass
options.says: protected includes package access, so Exporter in com.example.billing reads it freely

options.text: Exporter compiles and diff doesn't, since a subclass elsewhere reads it only through its own type
options.says: Exporter shares Invoice's package; diff reads other.totalCents through an Invoice from another package, which javac refuses

options.text: diff compiles and Exporter doesn't, since inside its package a protected member is open to subclasses only
options.says: protected includes package access, and diff's read through an Invoice is the one javac refuses

origin.section: protected Reaches a Subclass in Another Package Only Through Its Own Type

concepts: An override may widen the access of the method it overrides but never narrow it.
In another package a subclass reaches a protected member only through references of its own type, while every class in the member's package reaches it freely.
super.m() runs the direct superclass's version without dispatch; a cast of this to a superclass is still dispatched to the object's override, and super.super does not exist.
